description: The machinery software runs on: Linux, servers, web servers and proxies (nginx), virtualization, containers (Docker, Kubernetes), the cloud, and delivery pipelines.

concepts.title: Infrastructure
concepts.summary: Everything under the application: machines, networks, storage, and the tools that keep them running. When it works nobody notices it, which is the whole job.

concepts.title: Linux
concepts.summary: An open operating system kernel that started as one student's project and now runs most servers, phones, and supercomputers. Its design, small tools that do one thing and connect together, shaped how infrastructure is built.

concepts.title: The Shell
concepts.summary: A text conversation with the operating system. Small commands connected by pipes turn into powerful programs, and anything you can type once you can write down and repeat.

concepts.title: Processes
concepts.summary: A running program with its own memory and identity. The operating system juggles thousands, giving each a slice of the processor and keeping them out of each other's way.

concepts.title: File Systems
concepts.summary: The scheme that turns a disk of numbered blocks into named files in folders. On Unix-like systems nearly everything, even devices, is exposed as a file, a simple idea that makes tools compose.

concepts.title: Permissions
concepts.summary: Who may read, write, or run each file: owner, group, everyone else. A modest set of bits that is the first line of separation between users and programs on a machine.

concepts.title: Servers
concepts.summary: A machine, or a program on one, whose job is to answer requests. The difference from your laptop is mostly expectation: it must be there at any hour, and stay up while nobody watches.

concepts.title: Web Servers
concepts.summary: Programs that wait on a port, accept HTTP requests, and send back pages or data. Serving a static file is easy; doing it for thousands of visitors at once is the craft.

concepts.title: nginx
concepts.summary: A web server built to handle huge numbers of connections at once, using an event loop instead of a thread per visitor. It's also the everyday choice for reverse proxying, load balancing, and terminating TLS.

concepts.title: Reverse Proxy
concepts.summary: A front door that accepts requests and passes them to the right server behind it. It can add TLS, caching, compression, and limits in one place, so the services behind it stay simple.

concepts.title: Load Balancing
concepts.summary: Spreading requests across several servers so none is overwhelmed and the failure of one doesn't take the site down. Simple strategies, like taking turns, get you surprisingly far.

concepts.title: SSH
concepts.summary: An encrypted way to log into another machine and run commands. It replaced older tools that sent passwords in the clear, and keys instead of passwords make it much harder to break into.

concepts.title: Virtualization
concepts.summary: Making one machine behave like many. Software pretends to be hardware, so separate systems can share one box without seeing each other, and machines become something you can copy and move.

concepts.title: Virtual Machines
concepts.summary: A whole computer simulated in software, with its own operating system on top of a slice of real hardware. Strongly isolated, and correspondingly heavy.

concepts.title: Containers
concepts.summary: Isolated processes that share the host's kernel but see their own files, network, and process list. Much lighter than a virtual machine, so hundreds can run on one server.

concepts.title: Docker
concepts.summary: The tool that made containers ordinary: describe an application and everything it needs in an image, and it runs the same on a laptop or a server. Shipping the environment along with the code cured a lot of it works on my machine.

concepts.title: Kubernetes
concepts.summary: A system that runs containers across many machines: it starts them, restarts the ones that fail, scales them up and down, and routes traffic among them. You declare what you want, and it works to make it so.

concepts.title: Namespaces
concepts.summary: A Linux feature that gives a process its own private view of the system: its own process list, network, and file tree. It's the trick that makes a container feel like a machine of its own.

concepts.title: cgroups
concepts.summary: Another Linux feature that puts a ceiling on how much processor, memory, and disk a group of processes may use. Namespaces control what a container can see; cgroups control what it can consume.

concepts.title: The Cloud
concepts.summary: Renting machines, storage, and services by the hour from someone else's data centers. You stop owning hardware and start managing a bill, trading control for the ability to scale in minutes.

concepts.title: Serverless
concepts.summary: You upload a function and the provider runs it only when a request arrives. There are still servers; you just no longer think about them, or pay for them while they sit idle.

concepts.title: CDNs
concepts.summary: Copies of your content placed on servers around the world, so each visitor fetches from somewhere nearby. It beats latency the only way possible: by shortening the distance.

concepts.title: CI/CD
concepts.summary: Every change is automatically built, tested, and, if it passes, shipped. It turns release from an event people dread into something small and routine.

concepts.title: Infrastructure as Code
concepts.summary: Describe servers and networks in files instead of clicking through consoles. The setup can then be reviewed, versioned, and rebuilt from nothing, like any other program.
